title: Fugue in E minor
blurb: The only two-voice fugue in either book. One line above and one below, so you hear every entry without trying. Start here.

title: Fugue in C minor
blurb: Three voices, a compact subject, a countersubject that returns nearly every time, and episodes spun from the subject's own tail. If you learn to hear one fugue, make it this one.

title: Fugue in D minor
blurb: Short, fast, three voices, and halfway through Bach turns the subject upside down. Switch on the entry brackets and watch the shape flip.

title: Fugue in F major
blurb: A 3/8 fugue that moves like a dance. The subject is long and nearly all stepwise, so each voice reads as a tune rather than a knot of figuration.

title: Fugue in B-flat major
blurb: Cheerful, three voices, and a subject that leaps about for nearly four bars before it finishes. At that length there is room for only a handful of entries.

title: Fugue in C major
blurb: Almost nothing but subject. Four voices, no regular countersubject, barely an episode anywhere; the entries pile up in stretto until there is no room left for anything else.

title: Fugue in G minor
blurb: Four voices, a short subject with a very definite rhythm, and a countersubject that sticks to it. Play it after the two-voice E minor and you can hear what the extra lines do.

title: Fugue in E major
blurb: Bach writing in an idiom that was already old when he was born. Long white notes, alla breve, four voices moving like a Renaissance motet.

title: Contrapunctus I
blurb: One subject, four voices, no tricks. It opens The Art of Fugue as plainly as it can, and everything else in the cycle is a variation on it.
